extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers interested in philosophy of science and conceptions of matter/ether
extracted.subtask_short: defining matter in philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for how to construct, use, and evaluate scientific conceptions (e.g., matter, ether, atom) so they coherently describe perceptual experience without illicit metaphysical projection. Emphasises the use of conceptual shorthand, caution about projecting concepts into phenomenal reality, and criteria for accepting model systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not project special conceptions into real phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: We have clearly no right first to project special conceptions into the world of real phenomena, and then to assert on the strength of this that matter... is impenetrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid taking a conceptual convenience or hypothesis (e.g., atomic impenetrability) and treating it as an empirical fact; alternative hypotheses may equally well account for observed phenomena. Treat such conceptions as tools for description, not as unquestioned ontological commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate perceptual description from metaphysical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of statements about the nature of matter shows that they are metaphysical — they attempt to describe something beyond sense-impression, beyond perception, and appear as dogmas or inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confine scientific claims to what can be inferred from perceptual experience and logical inference; mark and treat with caution any statements that assert realities beyond sense-impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as description by conceptual shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is a description of perceptual experience by aid of conceptual shorthand, the symbols of this shorthand being in general ideal limits to perceptual processes, and as such having no exact perceptual equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conceptual models (symbols, ideal limits) to summarise and correlate sensory data; remember these models are not literal perceptual entities but tools to systematise experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conceptual matter from metaphysical substratum
rubrics_metrics.description: If we choose to term the moving things of the conceptual chart matter, there can be no objection to the term, provided we carefully distinguish this conceptual matter from any metaphysical ideas of matter as the substratum of sense-impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when using 'matter' in the conceptual/model sense (geometrical ideals with motions) versus the metaphysical sense (imperceptible substratum); avoid conflating the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler symbolic descriptions when they increase explanatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduction of 'matter to non-matter in motion' is so important as a possible simplification of our scientific analysis of phenomena that we must devote a few pages to its discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theoretical reduction that simplifies and unifies descriptions (e.g., expressing diverse sense-impressions via motions in a single medium) is valuable; pursue such simplifications provided they remain coherent with perceptual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat ether as a conceptual medium unless empirically warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first place, the ether is a pure conception by aid of which we correlate in conceptual space various motions... physicists project it into the phenomenal world and assert its real existence. There seems to be just as much, or little, logic in this assertion as in the postulate that there is a real substratum, matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ether as a tool to symbolise correlations of motion and phenomena; be cautious about asserting its phenomenal existence without empirical support and note its metaphysical status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness (sense-impression) is not a necessary characteristic of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to grasp how the sense-impression of hardness can tell us more of the nature of matter than the sense-impression of softness might be supposed to do... there are many things popularly termed matter and are certainly not hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not define 'matter' primarily by muscular sense-impressions like hardness; consider broader perceptual properties (weight, motion, filling space) and conceptual descriptions in physical terms (e.g., accelerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express sensory impressions in physical/mechanical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Muscular sense-impressions which we shall see are conceived by science to be describable in terms of the relative acceleration of certain parts of our body and of external bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate qualitative sense-impressions (e.g., hardness) into measurable physical descriptors (relative acceleration, forces) when building scientific explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge conceptual limits (perfect fluid, perfect jelly, rigid body) as idealisations
rubrics_metrics.description: An incompressible substance is merely a conceptual limit which has not its equivalent in the world of phenomena... Such a fluid is termed a perfect fluid... the perfectly rigid body is a conceptual limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise ideal models (perfect fluid/jelly/rigid body) as limiting cases useful for theory but not exact representations of perceptual reality; avoid treating them as literal phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile different conceptual models when both are used in same investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicists conceive the ether incompressible, but for some purposes they appear to treat it as a perfect fluid, for other purposes as a perfect jelly... we are compelled to try and find some reconciliation between these two conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a field uses multiple idealised models to explain different phenomena (e.g., fluid-like vs jelly-like ether), seek an overarching conception or explicit criteria for when each model applies to avoid contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanistic/types-of-motion hypotheses to account for properties (motion-stiffening)
rubrics_metrics.description: By aid of vortex-motion, or spinning elements of liquid in a liquid, we are able to conceive a liquid stiffened up to a required degree of resistance to sliding strain... a certain type of motion may suffice to stiffen a body not otherwise stiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how particular motion types in a medium can produce emergent material-like properties (e.g., stiffness, resistance) and use physical analogies (spinning tops, smoke-rings) as heuristic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses are justified if they enable resumption of perceptual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: From our standpoint, [ether and atom] are justified as conceptions if they enable us to resume our perceptual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt hypotheses that summarise and systematise observed phenomena even if they posit conceptual entities, but evaluate them on how well they reconstruct perceptual data and predictive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical rigour safeguards against frivolous metaphysical speculation (higher-dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessary mathematical equipment required for genuine research in the field of higher-dimensioned space will at any rate act as a safeguard against over light-hearted expeditions 'beyond the sensible'!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require appropriate mathematical tools and rigour before accepting speculative extensions (e.g., higher-dimensional spaces) to ensure they are substantive rather than metaphysical flights of fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model acceptance requires wide-reaching descriptive power
rubrics_metrics.description: No model dynamical system for the atom has as yet been shown to have such a wide-reaching power of describing our perceptual experience that it has passed from the field of imagination and become a current symbol of scientific shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a conceptual model (e.g., vortex-atom, ether-squirt) to be accepted, it must demonstrate broad explanatory and descriptive power across perceptual phenomena; otherwise it remains speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about projecting motion as phenomenal reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion is a pure conception, which may describe perceptual changes, but cannot be projected into the phenomenal world without involving us in inexplicable difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat motion primarily as a conceptual tool to relate sense-impressions; be wary of reifying motion as an unobserved phenomenal substance without resolving attendant paradoxes (e.g., ultimate moving elements).
